title: PMI Professional in Business Analysis (PMI-PBA)

exam.scoring: Pass/fail against a scaled passing score

content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the PMI-PBA exam content outline (five domains and task/enabler structure). Not a capture of past questions.

items.stem: A retail chain has seen online revenue fall for three consecutive quarters, and the sponsor wants to know what to do before committing budget. What should the business analyst do FIRST?
options: Perform a situation assessment to define the problem and its root causes
Recommend replacing the e-commerce platform immediately
Write detailed functional requirements for a new website
Ask the development team to build a mobile application
items.explanation: A needs assessment begins by understanding the problem and its causes before proposing any solution. Jumping to a platform replacement or new features assumes the cause and risks solving the wrong problem.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A sponsor requests a new executive dashboard but cannot explain which business problem it should solve. What is the MOST appropriate action for the business analyst?
options: Record the dashboard as an approved requirement and move on
Clarify the underlying business problem and desired outcomes before defining the solution
Build the dashboard exactly as requested to satisfy the sponsor
Escalate the request to the PMO for a decision
items.explanation: The business analyst must establish the problem and outcomes first so the solution is justified. Building or baselining an undefined request risks delivering something of no value, and escalation avoids the analysis needed.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business analyst is preparing a business case for a proposed system. Which content is MOST essential to justify the investment?
options: Marketing brochures from the preferred vendor
The personal preference of the chief information officer
Quantified costs, benefits, and risks that demonstrate expected value
The number of meetings held with each department
items.explanation: A business case justifies investment through quantified costs, benefits, and risks. Meeting counts, vendor brochures, and personal preferences are not evidence of value and cannot support a defensible decision.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: An organization wants to move from its current manual process to an automated future state. Which artifact best describes what must change?
options: A resource-loaded project schedule
A software test plan
A stakeholder communication matrix
A gap analysis comparing current and desired capabilities
items.explanation: A gap analysis identifies the differences between the current and future states so the change can be scoped. Schedules, test plans, and communication matrices support execution but do not define what must change.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A proposed solution looks attractive but its technical feasibility is unknown. What should the business analyst do?
options: Conduct a feasibility assessment covering technical, financial, and operational factors
Approve the solution and resolve technical issues during development
Discard the idea because feasibility is uncertain
Ask the vendor to guarantee the result in writing
items.explanation: Feasibility must be assessed across technical, financial, and operational dimensions before commitment. Proceeding blindly, abandoning a viable idea, or relying on a vendor guarantee all substitute hope for analysis.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Executives must compare two competing initiatives that have different costs and timelines. Which analysis BEST supports the decision?
options: The order in which the ideas were submitted
A cost-benefit analysis showing return on investment for each option
A list of features requested by each department
The number of stakeholders who prefer each option
items.explanation: Investment choices are supported by cost-benefit analysis and return on investment. Feature lists, popularity, and submission order are not valid financial or strategic selection criteria.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business analyst is asked to define the difference between a business problem and a business opportunity. Which statement is correct?
options: A problem belongs to operations, while an opportunity belongs to strategy
A problem requires a project, while an opportunity requires none
A problem is an adverse situation to correct, while an opportunity is a favorable circumstance to exploit
A problem always costs money, while an opportunity never does
items.explanation: A problem is a negative condition needing correction and an opportunity is a positive condition worth exploiting. Cost, organizational ownership, and the need for a project do not distinguish the two concepts.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Before launching a major process change, leadership asks whether the organization can absorb it. Which assessment should the business analyst perform?
options: A network bandwidth study
A vendor financial audit
A code review of the legacy system
An organizational readiness assessment of culture, skills, and capacity for change
items.explanation: Organizational readiness assesses whether culture, skills, and capacity can support the change. Technical, vendor, and code reviews do not address the organization's ability to adopt a new way of working.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A company wants to know whether its customer service performance is competitive. What should the business analyst do?
options: Benchmark current performance against industry peers and best practices
Copy a competitor's entire operating model without analysis
Assume current performance is adequate
Survey only internal managers about their feelings
items.explanation: Benchmarking compares performance to peers and best practices to reveal gaps. Blind copying, unfounded assumptions, and internal opinion alone do not establish competitive position.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business analyst must articulate why a proposed solution is worth pursuing. Which statement BEST expresses the value proposition?
options: The project's planned delivery milestones
A concise description of the benefits the solution delivers and the needs it satisfies
A list of technologies the solution will use
The development team's preferred architecture
items.explanation: A value proposition connects the solution to the benefits it delivers and needs it satisfies. Technology choices, architecture, and milestones are implementation details, not a statement of value.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: To understand how work is actually performed today, the business analyst interviews staff and maps the workflow. Which technique is being applied?
options: Benefits realization
Risk response planning
Current-state process modeling
Future-state prototyping
items.explanation: Mapping the workflow as it exists today is current-state process modeling. Prototyping addresses the future state, while benefits realization and risk response occur in later phases of the lifecycle.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Stakeholders disagree about what the solution should achieve. What should the business analyst do to define the future state?
options: Let the loudest stakeholder define the outcome
Postpone the discussion until development begins
Adopt the vendor's default configuration as the future state
Facilitate agreement on measurable desired outcomes and the capabilities needed to reach them
items.explanation: The future state is defined by agreed, measurable outcomes and required capabilities. Deferring, defaulting to a vendor, or yielding to the loudest voice leaves the target undefined and contested.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A support desk has a high volume of repeat complaints, and management wants the true cause identified. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
options: Root cause analysis such as the five whys or a fishbone diagram
Cost-benefit analysis
A Monte Carlo simulation
A resource histogram
items.explanation: Root cause analysis techniques such as the five whys and fishbone diagrams trace symptoms to their source. Cost-benefit, simulation, and resource tools address financial, schedule, and staffing questions instead.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: The sponsor keeps adding ideas that fall outside the original need. What should the business analyst do?
options: Stop documenting scope to keep flexibility
Define and confirm the solution scope so out-of-scope ideas go through change control
Quietly accept every addition to avoid conflict
Remove the sponsor from the project
items.explanation: A confirmed solution scope gives a reference point so new ideas are evaluated rather than absorbed. Accepting everything causes scope creep, and removing the sponsor or abandoning documentation are not viable controls.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business analyst finds that staff lack the data skills required for a new analytics platform. What has the analyst identified?
options: A coding defect
A network outage
A capability gap between the current workforce and the future-state need
A hardware constraint
items.explanation: A shortfall in the skills needed for the future state is a capability gap. Hardware, defects, and outages are technical conditions, not gaps between current and required organizational capability.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Several business needs compete for the same limited funding. How should the business analyst help leaders choose?
options: Fund every need equally to keep everyone happy
Choose the need with the largest number of requesters
Defer all decisions until next year
Prioritize needs by their contribution to strategic value and urgency
items.explanation: Needs should be prioritized by strategic value and urgency. Equal funding dilutes impact, request counts measure popularity rather than value, and indefinite deferral avoids the decision.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: The business case should demonstrate that options were compared. What should the business analyst include?
options: An analysis of viable alternatives with their costs, benefits, and risks
Only the preferred option with no comparison
A single vendor quote
A summary of team preferences
items.explanation: A credible business case compares viable alternatives on costs, benefits, and risks. Presenting one option, a lone quote, or team preferences does not demonstrate that a sound choice was made.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A public-sector project will not generate direct revenue but will improve citizen access. How should the business analyst treat this benefit?
options: Exclude the project because it has no return on investment
Represent non-financial benefits qualitatively with clear measures in the business case
Ignore any benefit that cannot be expressed in currency
Estimate a fake revenue figure to justify funding
items.explanation: Non-financial benefits are represented with clear qualitative measures so value is still visible. Ignoring them, fabricating revenue, or excluding the project misrepresents the true rationale for the investment.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: The business case should justify action by addressing the alternative. Which statement captures the cost of inaction?
options: The number of project meetings
The chosen programming language
The consequences and costs the organization avoids by acting now
The salary of the business analyst
items.explanation: The cost of inaction is the harm the organization avoids or incurs by acting or delaying. Analyst salary, meeting counts, and technology choices do not express the consequence of doing nothing.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A regulator has issued a new data privacy rule, and the business analyst must respond. What drives this need?
options: A discretionary feature request from marketing
A preference of the development team
An opportunity to increase advertising
A mandatory compliance requirement and the associated risk of non-compliance
items.explanation: Regulatory obligations create mandatory needs with legal and financial risk if unmet. Discretionary requests, developer preferences, and advertising opportunities are not compliance drivers.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A proposed initiative aligns poorly with the organization's stated strategy. What should the business analyst recommend?
options: Flag the misalignment in the business case for the sponsor to reconsider
Proceed because the requester is senior
Hide the misalignment to speed approval
Redefine the strategy to match the initiative
items.explanation: Misalignment should be surfaced so decision makers can weigh the investment against strategy. Proceeding on seniority, concealing the issue, or rewriting strategy to fit a project inverts the proper relationship.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Two problems affect customers, but one causes far greater harm. What should the business analyst assess to guide prioritization?
options: Which team owns each problem
The magnitude and impact of each problem
Which problem was reported first
Which problem is easier to solve
items.explanation: Prioritization is guided by the magnitude and impact of each problem. Reporting order, ease of solving, and ownership are not measures of how much harm a problem causes.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business case relies on assumptions about future demand. What should the business analyst do?
options: Omit assumptions to keep the case simple
Use only the most optimistic assumption
Validate the assumptions with stakeholders and state the risks if they prove wrong
Present the assumptions as guaranteed facts
items.explanation: Assumptions should be validated and their consequences if wrong should be stated. Presenting them as facts, omitting them, or using only the optimistic case hides uncertainty from decision makers.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: An executive wants benefits delivered as early as possible. Which consideration should the business analyst add to the business case?
options: The color scheme of the user interface
The length of each development sprint
The developer's years of experience
The expected time to value and opportunities for incremental delivery
items.explanation: Time to value and incremental delivery show when benefits begin. Interface styling, sprint length, and individual experience do not address the speed at which value is realized.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: Who should be named in the business case as accountable for realizing the benefits?
options: The business owner who will use the solution to achieve the outcomes
The business analyst who wrote the document
The vendor who supplies the software
The tester who verified the release
items.explanation: The business owner is accountable for using the solution to achieve the outcomes. The analyst documents, the vendor supplies, and the tester verifies, but none of them owns the benefit.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A firm suspects its product no longer meets customer expectations. Which analysis should the business analyst perform?
options: A review of employee vacation balances
Customer and market analysis to understand needs and competitive position
An inventory count of office supplies
A network latency test
items.explanation: Customer and market analysis reveals whether the product still satisfies needs and how it compares to competitors. Inventory, network, and leave-balance reviews do not address product-market fit.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A project cannot exceed a fixed regulatory deadline, and the business analyst must record it. This is an example of what?
options: A benefit to be realized
A risk to be transferred
A constraint that limits solution options
An assumption to be validated later
items.explanation: A fixed deadline is a constraint that limits the options available. It is not an assumption, a benefit, or a risk to be transferred; these are distinct concepts in business analysis.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A well-written problem statement is needed before solution design. What should it contain?
options: The chosen technology and vendor
A detailed test script
The project budget breakdown
A clear description of the current adverse condition and its business impact
items.explanation: A problem statement describes the current adverse condition and its business impact. Technology choices, test scripts, and budget details belong to solution design and planning, not problem definition.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A new technology could reduce processing costs significantly. How should the business analyst frame this?
options: As a business opportunity with a value hypothesis to be assessed
As a mandatory requirement
As a defect to be corrected
As a personal initiative of the analyst
items.explanation: A potential improvement is framed as an opportunity with a value hypothesis to test. It is not yet a requirement or defect, and it should never be presented as a personal initiative of the analyst.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: The needs assessment is complete and approved. What should the business analyst do NEXT?
options: Close the project
Plan stakeholder engagement and elicitation to develop and refine requirements
Stop work until development is scheduled
Begin coding the solution
items.explanation: Once the need is understood and approved, the next step is to engage stakeholders and elicit requirements. Coding, closing the project, or idling skips the essential business analysis work.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Needs Assessment

items.stem: A business analyst begins a new initiative and needs to determine who is affected by the change. What should the analyst do FIRST?
options: Start writing requirements from the sponsor's request
Order new software licenses
Identify all stakeholders and analyze their interests and influence
Send a project kickoff email to the whole company
items.explanation: Stakeholder identification and analysis comes first so the right people are involved and informed. Broadcasting, writing requirements, and purchasing hardware all presume an understanding of stakeholders that has not yet been built.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A project has many stakeholders with differing levels of authority. Which tool helps the business analyst plan engagement?
options: A Gantt chart of development tasks
A financial statement
A network diagram
A power and interest grid that classifies stakeholders by influence and concern
items.explanation: A power and interest grid classifies stakeholders by influence and concern to tailor engagement. Schedules, financial statements, and network diagrams serve other purposes and do not guide stakeholder strategy.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of a stakeholder register?
options: To record each stakeholder's role, interests, influence, and engagement needs
To track the project budget by department
To list the software modules to be built
To schedule the test cycles
items.explanation: A stakeholder register records roles, interests, influence, and engagement needs. Budget tracking, module lists, and test scheduling are handled by other artifacts and are not its purpose.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A key stakeholder is influential but currently resistant to the change. What should the business analyst do?
options: Ignore the resistance until go-live
Develop targeted engagement actions to understand and address the resistance
Exclude the stakeholder from communications
Report the stakeholder to the sponsor for discipline
items.explanation: Influential resistance is addressed through targeted engagement that uncovers and resolves concerns. Excluding, punishing, or ignoring the stakeholder increases the risk that the change fails.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A communication plan is being developed. What should determine the methods and frequency of communication?
options: The cheapest available tool
A fixed weekly email to everyone regardless of need
Stakeholder information needs, preferences, and the criticality of the message
The business analyst's personal schedule
items.explanation: Effective communication planning is driven by stakeholder needs, preferences, and message criticality. Personal convenience, cost alone, and one-size-fits-all blasts do not meet stakeholder needs.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: The sponsor's approval is required to baseline requirements, but the sponsor is often unavailable. What should the business analyst do?
options: Approve the baseline without the sponsor
Ask the development team to approve instead
Delay the project indefinitely
Negotiate and document an approval approach and delegation that fits the sponsor's availability
items.explanation: The analyst should agree a practical approval and delegation approach with the sponsor. Self-approval or transferring authority to developers violates governance, and indefinite delay is unnecessary.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Two departments have conflicting expectations of the same solution. What should the business analyst do?
options: Facilitate a joint discussion to surface the conflict and negotiate a mutually acceptable outcome
Support the department with the larger budget
Document both expectations and let developers choose
Escalate immediately without any analysis
items.explanation: Facilitation lets stakeholders surface and resolve conflicting expectations directly. Favoring a budget, offloading the decision to developers, or escalating before analysis all avoid the analyst's responsibility.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A business analyst must gain cooperation from stakeholders over whom the analyst has no direct authority. Which approach is BEST?
options: Wait for them to volunteer help
Build relationships and demonstrate how the change serves their interests
Threaten escalation to their managers
Ignore stakeholders who lack authority
items.explanation: Influence without authority is built through relationships and shared benefit. Threats damage trust, ignoring stakeholders loses their input, and passive waiting rarely yields cooperation.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Subject matter experts are needed to supply detailed knowledge. How should the business analyst engage them?
options: Replace them with the business analyst's own assumptions
Ask them to write all the requirements alone
Involve them early and define their expected contributions and availability
Contact them only after the build is finished
items.explanation: Subject matter experts should be involved early with clear expectations of contribution and availability. Late contact, substitute assumptions, and delegating all requirements to them each undermine the analysis.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Who is MOST appropriate to formally approve the final set of requirements?
options: The business analyst who authored them
The most vocal end user
The software vendor
The authorized business sponsor or designated approver
items.explanation: Formal approval belongs to the authorized sponsor or designated approver. Authors, vocal users, and vendors may contribute but do not hold the accountability for approving requirements.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A business analyst wants ongoing input from users during the project. What should be established?
options: A feedback mechanism such as representatives, reviews, or surveys
A rule that users may not contact the team
A single communication at project close
A policy of verbal-only updates
items.explanation: A defined feedback mechanism keeps user input flowing throughout the project. Blocking contact, communicating only at close, or relying on untracked verbal updates prevents timely course correction.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A critical message must reach a dispersed audience consistently and be retrievable later. Which communication method is BEST?
options: A casual comment during lunch
A written communication sent through an agreed channel and stored for reference
A rumor passed along the hallway
An unrecorded phone call
items.explanation: Critical messages need a consistent written channel with a retrievable record. Hallway rumors, unrecorded calls, and casual comments are neither consistent nor documented for later reference.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A stakeholder keeps requesting additions late in the project. What should the business analyst do?
options: Refuse all changes without explanation
Redesign the solution secretly
Guide the request through the change control process and assess its impact
Accept every request to preserve the relationship
items.explanation: Late requests should flow through change control so their impact is assessed. Accepting everything causes scope creep, blanket refusal ignores valid needs, and secret redesign bypasses governance.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A regulatory body must be kept informed of compliance progress. How should this stakeholder be treated?
options: As a low-priority stakeholder to contact only if asked
As a stakeholder with no communication needs
As an obstacle to be managed around
As a high-priority stakeholder with formal, scheduled reporting obligations
items.explanation: Regulators require formal, scheduled reporting and are high priority. Downgrading them, assuming no communication needs, or treating them as obstacles risks compliance and penalties.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: The business analyst needs to clarify who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed for requirements decisions. Which tool applies?
options: A RACI matrix
A burn-down chart
A data dictionary
A network topology diagram
items.explanation: A RACI matrix clarifies who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed. Burn-down, data dictionary, and network diagrams track progress, data definitions, and infrastructure instead.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A stakeholder has moved from resistant to supportive over the project. Which tool records this change in engagement?
options: A capacity plan
A stakeholder engagement assessment matrix tracking current and desired engagement
A risk register of technical issues
A test summary report
items.explanation: An engagement assessment matrix records current versus desired engagement and shows movement over time. Risk, test, and capacity artifacts do not track stakeholder attitudes.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Mismatched expectations about delivery date are causing friction. What should the business analyst do?
options: Avoid discussing dates entirely
Blame the schedule on the developers
Confirm and communicate a shared, realistic expectation with the stakeholders
Promise every date each stakeholder wants
items.explanation: Aligning stakeholders on a shared, realistic expectation resolves friction. Overpromising, avoiding the topic, and shifting blame all leave expectations mismatched and trust degraded.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A stakeholder issue cannot be resolved at the working level. What should the business analyst do?
options: Conceal the issue to avoid attention
Resolve it by ignoring the stakeholder
Post the conflict publicly to force a decision
Follow the agreed escalation path while keeping stakeholders informed
items.explanation: Unresolved issues follow the agreed escalation path with ongoing communication. Concealment, ignoring the stakeholder, and public forcing are unprofessional and damage relationships.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Determining how often to communicate with a stakeholder should be based on what?
options: The stakeholder's information needs and the project's risk and change rate
A fixed monthly cadence for everyone
The business analyst's workload
The number of emails already sent
items.explanation: Communication frequency should reflect information needs and project risk and change. Uniform cadence ignores differences, and analyst workload or past email volume are not valid drivers.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A previous project failed partly because a key stakeholder was not engaged early. What should the business analyst do on the new project?
options: Delegate all engagement to the vendor
Identify and engage key stakeholders from the start and learn from past lessons
Repeat the previous approach exactly
Wait for stakeholders to make contact
items.explanation: Lessons from the past should drive early identification and engagement of key stakeholders. Repeating the mistake, waiting passively, or delegating engagement to a vendor repeats the failure.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: An executive sponsor can advocate for the change and help overcome resistance. What role does this represent?
options: A blocker who should be excluded
A tester of the final product
A champion who actively promotes the solution to others
A passive observer with no involvement
items.explanation: A sponsor who advocates for the change acts as a champion. Passive observers, excluded blockers, and testers do not perform the advocacy role that helps the solution succeed.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: Actual end users rarely attend meetings, yet their acceptance is vital. What should the business analyst do?
options: Speak for users based on assumptions
Exclude users until acceptance testing
Rely only on management's view of user needs
Include representative end users in elicitation and validation activities
items.explanation: Representative end users should participate in elicitation and validation so their real needs shape the solution. Assumptions, late involvement, and management-only views miss critical user requirements.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: How can the business analyst confirm that stakeholder engagement is effective?
options: By checking participation, feedback, agreement, and progress toward shared goals
By counting the number of meetings held
By measuring the length of emails sent
By assuming silence means agreement
items.explanation: Engagement effectiveness shows in participation, feedback, agreement, and goal progress. Meeting counts, email length, and interpreting silence as consent are weak or misleading indicators.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A new stakeholder joins the project midway. What should the business analyst do?
options: Restart the entire project
Perform stakeholder analysis for the new participant and update engagement and communication plans
Ignore the change because plans are already set
Add the name without any analysis
items.explanation: New stakeholders require analysis and updates to engagement and communication plans. Ignoring them, adding them without analysis, or restarting the project are disproportionate to a normal change.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A high-power, low-interest stakeholder could become disruptive if surprised. What engagement approach is appropriate?
options: Ignore them completely
Give them ownership of all decisions
Keep the stakeholder adequately informed and manage their concerns without overloading them
Send every detail daily regardless of interest
items.explanation: High-power, low-interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied with adequate information without overload. Daily detail, complete neglect, and handing over all decisions all misread their needs.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Stakeholder Engagement

items.stem: A business analyst must choose an elicitation technique for a topic that is sensitive and poorly understood. What should guide the choice?
options: The technique the analyst used last time
The cheapest technique available
The technique the vendor recommends regardless of fit
The nature of the information needed, stakeholder characteristics, and available time and resources
items.explanation: Technique selection depends on the information needed, stakeholder characteristics, and constraints. Habit, cost alone, or vendor preference without fit analysis usually yields poor elicitation results.

items.stem: Before conducting elicitation sessions, what should the business analyst do?
options: Define objectives, select participants, and prepare logistics and materials
Begin interviewing the first available person
Assume stakeholders will provide complete information spontaneously
Skip preparation to save time
items.explanation: Preparation establishes objectives, participants, logistics, and materials for effective elicitation. Interviewing at random, assuming complete information, and skipping preparation reduce the quality of results.

items.stem: Detailed, confidential information is needed from one expert. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
options: A group brainstorming session
A one-on-one interview
A large open forum
An anonymous survey to the whole company
items.explanation: One-on-one interviews are suited to detailed, confidential information from a single expert. Forums, company-wide surveys, and group brainstorms lack the privacy and depth required here.

items.stem: Multiple stakeholders must reach agreement on a complex process. Which technique is BEST?
options: A yes-or-no email poll
Reading the process manual alone
A facilitated workshop with structured activities
Separate hallway conversations
items.explanation: A facilitated workshop brings stakeholders together to reach agreement on complex topics. Side conversations, binary polls, and solo document reading cannot build consensus among multiple parties.

items.stem: The business analyst wants to capture shared perceptions and reactions among a small group of similar users. Which technique applies?
options: A user acceptance test
A cost-benefit analysis
A data migration run
A focus group
items.explanation: A focus group elicits shared perceptions and reactions from a small, similar group. Acceptance testing, cost-benefit analysis, and data migration occur elsewhere in the lifecycle and serve different purposes.

items.stem: Documents describing how work is done may not match reality. Which technique reveals actual behavior?
options: Observation or job shadowing of users as they work
Reviewing the organizational chart
Reading the annual report
Interviewing only the department head
items.explanation: Observation and job shadowing reveal what people actually do rather than what documents say. Org charts, annual reports, and single interviews do not capture real work behavior.

items.stem: Information is needed from many geographically dispersed stakeholders quickly. Which technique is MOST suitable?
options: Unstructured observation
A structured questionnaire or survey
A single in-person workshop with everyone
A series of one-on-one interviews over months
items.explanation: A structured survey reaches many dispersed stakeholders quickly. A single in-person workshop, months of interviews, and unstructured observation cannot efficiently cover a large, distributed group.

items.stem: A business analyst reviews existing policies, manuals, and system documentation to understand requirements. Which technique is being used?
options: Facilitated workshops
Focus groups
Document analysis
Prototyping
items.explanation: Reviewing existing policies, manuals, and documentation is document analysis. Prototyping, workshops, and focus groups involve interaction with people rather than review of written materials.

items.stem: A team needs to generate many creative ideas to address a problem. Which technique is appropriate?
options: A root cause analysis only
A cost-benefit analysis
A network diagram
Brainstorming with rules that encourage open contribution
items.explanation: Brainstorming with ground rules generates a broad set of creative ideas. Root cause, cost-benefit, and network tools analyze or represent information rather than ideate widely.

items.stem: Stakeholders struggle to describe what they want in a screen. Which technique helps them react to a concrete representation?
options: Prototyping
Benchmarking
A resource histogram
A RACI matrix
items.explanation: Prototyping gives stakeholders something concrete to react to so they can refine requirements. Benchmarking, resource histograms, and RACI matrices do not represent a user interface.

items.stem: An existing legacy system has no documentation, and its behavior must be understood. Which technique applies?
options: Benchmarking against competitors
Reverse engineering to infer the system's logic and data
Focus groups with executives
A survey of new hires
items.explanation: Reverse engineering infers the logic and data of an undocumented system. Executive focus groups, new-hire surveys, and competitive benchmarking cannot expose an undocumented system's behavior.

items.stem: Requirements must be defined for how two systems exchange data. Which elicitation technique is MOST relevant?
options: A process audit
A lessons-learned workshop
Interface analysis of the data and interactions between systems
A customer satisfaction survey
items.explanation: Interface analysis examines the data and interactions between systems to define integration requirements. Satisfaction surveys, process audits, and lessons-learned sessions address other concerns.

items.stem: A business analyst is planning elicitation and must decide what to elicit first. What should guide sequencing?
options: The order in which stakeholders are alphabetized
The business analyst's personal preference
The vendor's implementation timeline
The business objectives and the highest-value, highest-uncertainty information
items.explanation: Elicitation sequencing should target the information with the highest value and uncertainty relative to objectives. Alphabetical order, personal preference, and vendor timelines do not prioritize learning.

items.stem: An elicitation session ends with unanswered questions. What should the business analyst do?
options: Record follow-up actions and schedule additional elicitation as needed
Declare the session a failure and stop
Guess the answers to move forward
Wait for stakeholders to volunteer information
items.explanation: Unanswered questions become documented follow-ups with additional elicitation scheduled. Stopping, guessing, or waiting passively leaves requirements incomplete and unverified.

items.stem: Elicited information from several sources conflicts. What should the business analyst do NEXT?
options: Discard the information and start over
Analyze the conflict, reconcile the sources, and confirm the agreed interpretation with stakeholders
Pick the answer from the most senior person and move on
Document all conflicting versions as requirements
items.explanation: Conflicts are resolved by analysis and reconciliation confirmed with stakeholders. Deferring to seniority, documenting contradictions as requirements, or discarding everything leaves the conflict unresolved.

items.stem: How should a business analyst confirm the accuracy of elicited requirements before baselining?
options: Have the developers confirm requirements instead of stakeholders
Skip confirmation to save time
Review and validate the results with the source stakeholders and obtain their agreement
Assume the notes are correct and proceed
items.explanation: Accuracy is confirmed by reviewing and validating results with the source stakeholders. Assumptions, developer confirmation, and skipped reviews do not verify that the captured information is correct.

items.stem: What is the purpose of obtaining stakeholder sign-off on elicitation results?
options: To transfer blame if requirements change
To satisfy a document-filing rule
To delay the project until everyone is free
To formally confirm a shared and accurate understanding of the elicited information
items.explanation: Sign-off confirms that stakeholders share and accept the elicited information. It is not about blame, filing, or delay; it is a checkpoint of mutual understanding before analysis continues.

items.stem: Key subject matter experts are too busy for a joint session. What should the business analyst do?
options: Schedule shorter targeted sessions and adapt techniques to their availability
Force them to attend a full-day workshop
Proceed without their input entirely
Escalate them to the sponsor for discipline
items.explanation: Adapting to availability with shorter targeted sessions still captures expert knowledge. Forcing attendance, skipping their input, or escalating for discipline harms relationships and results.

items.stem: A survey is being designed. Which practice improves data quality?
options: Make questions intentionally vague
Write clear, unbiased questions and pilot them with a small sample
Use leading questions to get desired answers
Include double-barreled questions to save space
items.explanation: Clear, unbiased questions tested in a pilot produce reliable data. Leading, double-barreled, and vague questions introduce bias and confuse respondents, degrading data quality.

items.stem: A workshop becomes dominated by one participant. What should the facilitator do?
options: End the workshop immediately
Ignore the imbalance
Apply ground rules and facilitation techniques to ensure balanced participation
Allow the dominant voice to set all decisions
items.explanation: Facilitators use ground rules and techniques to balance participation. Letting one person dominate, ending the session, or ignoring the imbalance excludes other stakeholders and skews results.

items.stem: Which listening behavior best supports effective elicitation?
options: Listening only for points that support a preconceived solution
Interrupting to speed the session
Taking no notes and relying on memory
Active listening with clarifying and confirming questions
items.explanation: Active listening with clarifying and confirming questions surfaces accurate information. Selective listening, interrupting, and relying on memory bias or lose important detail.

items.stem: The business analyst needs to move from broad understanding to specific detail during an interview. Which questioning approach is BEST?
options: Start with open-ended questions, then use closed questions to confirm specifics
Use only closed questions throughout
Use only rhetorical questions
Avoid questions and rely on assumptions
items.explanation: Opening with open-ended questions explores the topic, and closed questions confirm specifics. Only-closed questions limit discovery, rhetorical questions gather no data, and avoiding questions yields assumptions.

items.stem: What should happen immediately after an elicitation session regarding the captured information?
options: Delete the notes to protect privacy
Document the results promptly in a clear, organized form
Rely on memory to reconstruct it weeks later
Share raw unedited notes as final requirements
items.explanation: Results should be documented promptly while the information is fresh and accurate. Memory fades, raw notes are not requirements, and deleting notes loses valuable elicited information.

items.stem: How can a business analyst validate understanding with an elicitation participant?
options: Send the notes only to the sponsor
Wait until acceptance testing to check
Restate and summarize what was heard and ask the participant to confirm or correct it
Assume agreement based on nodding
items.explanation: Restating and summarizing lets the participant confirm or correct the analyst's understanding. Nodding, sponsor-only review, and waiting until testing all delay or skip validation.

items.stem: Who should be selected to participate in elicitation?
options: Only the most senior managers
Only the people easiest to schedule
Anyone who happens to be available
Representative stakeholders who collectively have the needed knowledge and authority
items.explanation: Participants should be selected for the knowledge and authority they collectively bring. Seniority alone, scheduling convenience, and random availability omit key perspectives and information.

items.stem: A workshop agenda has too many topics for the time allowed. What should the business analyst do?
options: Prioritize topics and timebox each segment, deferring low-priority items
Extend the meeting indefinitely
Cut all discussion of controversial topics
Let the meeting run without an agenda
items.explanation: Prioritizing and timeboxing keeps the workshop focused and productive. Endless extension exhausts participants, avoiding controversy leaves issues unresolved, and no agenda loses control of the session.

items.stem: Stakeholders fear that candid feedback will be attributed to them. Which approach can increase honesty?
options: Threaten consequences for criticism
Offer anonymity or confidentiality where appropriate
Require names on every comment
Publicly rank the feedback by source
items.explanation: Anonymity or confidentiality reduces fear and encourages candor. Mandatory names, public ranking of sources, and threats suppress honest input and reduce the quality of elicited information.

items.stem: A solution affects several departments, and each sees only part of the process. What elicitation format is BEST?
options: A single survey to one department
Observation of one team only
A cross-functional workshop to build a shared end-to-end view
Independent isolated interviews with no sharing
items.explanation: A cross-functional workshop assembles all parties to build a shared end-to-end view. Isolated interviews, single-department surveys, and observing one team leave critical interfaces and gaps unseen.

items.stem: Experienced staff perform tasks from habit and cannot easily explain them. Which technique captures this tacit knowledge?
options: A theoretical feasibility study
A financial audit
A network diagram
Observation of the staff performing the work
items.explanation: Observing staff as they work captures tacit knowledge they cannot articulate. Feasibility studies, financial audits, and network diagrams analyze other matters and do not reveal habitual work practices.

items.stem: Two stakeholders give contradictory requirements. What should the business analyst do?
options: Facilitate resolution by clarifying needs and negotiating a shared requirement
Adopt both without analysis and let them coexist
Choose one at random
Drop the conflicting topic entirely
items.explanation: Facilitating resolution turns contradictory inputs into one negotiated requirement. Adopting both leaves unresolved contradictions, random choice is indefensible, and dropping the topic leaves a gap.

items.stem: After elicitation, the business analyst wants stakeholders to review outputs before they become requirements. What is the BEST approach?
options: Only share with the sponsor
Distribute a clear summary for review and confirm corrections before baselining
Treat drafts as final immediately
Keep the outputs secret until development
items.explanation: A clear summary reviewed and corrected by stakeholders ensures accuracy before baselining. Treating drafts as final, secrecy, and sponsor-only review bypass the people who provided the information.

items.stem: Why should elicited information be traceable to its source?
options: To inflate the documentation volume
To satisfy a formatting rule
To support verification, manage changes, and understand the rationale behind requirements
To assign blame when issues arise
items.explanation: Traceability to the source supports verification, change management, and understanding of rationale. Blame, documentation volume, and formatting rules are not the goal of traceability.

items.stem: At the close of an elicitation activity, what should the business analyst confirm with participants?
options: That no further communication will occur
That all requirements are frozen forever
That participants will not be contacted again
That objectives were met, results are understood, and next steps are agreed
items.explanation: Closing an elicitation activity confirms objectives met, shared understanding, and agreed next steps. Promising no further contact, permanent freezing, or excluding follow-up contradicts iterative elicitation.

items.stem: How should a business analyst decide when enough elicitation has been done?
options: When the information needed to define the solution is sufficiently complete and validated
When a fixed number of sessions has been held regardless of content
When stakeholders stop replying to emails
When the budget is nearly exhausted
items.explanation: Elicitation is complete when the needed information is sufficiently complete and validated. A fixed session count, silence, or budget exhaustion are not indicators that requirements are adequately understood.

items.stem: A first round of elicitation raises new questions about scope. What should the business analyst do?
options: Delegate all open questions to developers
Plan an additional elicitation iteration to resolve the open questions
Ignore the new questions
Freeze scope and refuse further elicitation
items.explanation: Elicitation is iterative, so new questions lead to another planned round. Ignoring questions, freezing scope prematurely, or delegating them to developers leaves requirements unresolved.

items.stem: A business analyst is analyzing facts and opinions gathered during elicitation to define requirements. What is the purpose of requirements analysis?
options: To begin coding the solution
To approve the project budget
To transform elicited information into a validated, agreed set of requirements
To collect more opinions from stakeholders
items.explanation: Requirements analysis turns elicited information into a validated, agreed set of requirements. Collecting more opinions is elicitation, while coding and budgeting belong to delivery and planning.

items.stem: A requirement states that the system shall allow customers to reset their own passwords. What kind of requirement is this?
options: A non-functional requirement about performance
A constraint on the project schedule
A business rule governing access policy
A functional requirement describing a capability the solution must provide
items.explanation: A statement that the system shall perform a specific behavior is a functional requirement. Performance is non-functional, and the statement is neither a schedule constraint nor a business rule.

items.stem: A requirement states that the system shall respond to any user query in under two seconds. What kind of requirement is this?
options: A non-functional requirement specifying a quality attribute
A functional requirement describing a feature
A business rule about access
A project assumption
items.explanation: Response time is a quality attribute, making this a non-functional requirement. It does not describe a feature, an access rule, or an assumption about the project environment.

items.stem: A requirement states that only managers may approve expenses above a set threshold. This is BEST classified as what?
options: A performance requirement
A business rule that constrains how the organization operates
A user interface requirement
A data migration requirement
items.explanation: A policy governing who may approve what is a business rule. Interface, migration, and performance requirements describe system qualities rather than organizational policy.

items.stem: A requirement includes the condition that must be true for a user story to be accepted. What is this condition called?
options: A change request
A risk response
An acceptance criterion that defines the condition of satisfaction
A project constraint
items.explanation: The condition that must be true for acceptance is an acceptance criterion. Constraints, change requests, and risk responses are distinct artifacts that do not define satisfaction of a story.

items.stem: The business analyst models how actors interact with the system to achieve goals. Which model is being created?
options: A data flow diagram of physical storage
A resource histogram
A network diagram
A use case model
items.explanation: Modeling actors and their goals against a system produces a use case model. Storage diagrams, resource histograms, and network diagrams represent data, staffing, and infrastructure instead.

items.stem: A business analyst diagrams the sequence of activities that transform inputs into outputs. Which model applies?
options: A process model such as a swimlane or activity diagram
A class diagram of objects
A cost-benefit model
A RACI chart
items.explanation: A sequence of activities transforming inputs to outputs is modeled with a process or activity diagram. Class diagrams model structure, and cost-benefit and RACI artifacts serve other purposes.

items.stem: The team needs to understand the entities, attributes, and relationships that the solution must store. Which model is appropriate?
options: A stakeholder map
A data model or entity-relationship diagram
A use case diagram
A Gantt chart
items.explanation: Entities, attributes, and relationships are represented in a data or entity-relationship model. Use case, Gantt, and stakeholder artifacts address interactions, schedules, and people instead.

items.stem: A business analyst must describe the valid states of an order and the allowed transitions between them. Which model is useful?
options: A resource calendar
A communication plan
A state diagram or state machine model
A pie chart
items.explanation: States and allowed transitions are captured in a state or state machine model. Pie charts, resource calendars, and communication plans do not represent lifecycle transitions of an entity.

items.stem: Stakeholders cannot articulate detailed requirements, but they can react to a draft screen. Which analysis technique helps refine requirements?
options: Cost-benefit analysis
Risk register analysis
Benchmarking
Prototyping to make requirements concrete and elicit feedback
items.explanation: Prototyping gives stakeholders a concrete artifact to react to, refining requirements. Cost-benefit, risk, and benchmarking analyses do not surface detailed interface expectations.

items.stem: Requirements must be categorized for release planning as must-have, should-have, could-have, and will-not-have. Which technique is being used?
options: MoSCoW prioritization
Monte Carlo analysis
Root cause analysis
Variance analysis
items.explanation: The must, should, could, and will-not categories are MoSCoW prioritization. Monte Carlo, root cause, and variance analysis address uncertainty, causation, and performance gaps.

items.stem: A business analyst must prioritize requirements when both business value and implementation risk vary. Which approach is BEST?
options: Prioritize alphabetically
Rank requirements by value against cost and risk so the highest-value items come first
Implement requirements in the order they were requested
Prioritize by the size of the requesting department
items.explanation: Prioritization should weigh value against cost and risk. Request order, department size, and alphabetical ordering carry no information about value or risk.

items.stem: What is the goal of requirements verification?
options: To estimate the project cost
To assign developers to tasks
To confirm that requirements are well-formed, complete, and consistent as written
To confirm the solution meets business needs once built
items.explanation: Verification confirms that requirements are well-formed, complete, and consistent. Confirming a built solution meets needs is validation, while cost and staffing are planning activities.

items.stem: What is the goal of requirements validation?
options: To check spelling and grammar only
To estimate the project schedule
To secure the software license
To confirm that the requirements accurately represent stakeholder needs and deliver value
items.explanation: Validation confirms that requirements accurately represent stakeholder needs and value. Proofreading, scheduling, and licensing are unrelated to ensuring the requirements are the right ones.

items.stem: A requirement states that the system shall be user friendly. What quality characteristic is violated?
options: It is ambiguous and not measurable
It is too short
It is a functional requirement
It is a business rule
items.explanation: User friendly is subjective and unmeasurable, so the requirement is ambiguous. Length, being functional, or being a business rule are not the defects present in this statement.

items.stem: A requirement states that the system shall be fast. Which issue should the business analyst correct?
options: The requirement is redundant
The requirement is not testable and needs a measurable threshold
The requirement is too detailed
The requirement is a constraint
items.explanation: Fast cannot be tested without a measurable threshold, so it must be quantified. The statement is not overly detailed, a constraint, or necessarily redundant; testability is the core defect.

items.stem: During review, the business analyst finds that requirements omit important scenarios. Which quality is lacking?
options: Testability
Feasibility
Completeness
Traceability
items.explanation: Missing important scenarios is a completeness defect. Traceability, testability, and feasibility are different quality characteristics and do not describe omitted content.

items.stem: Two requirements contradict each other about the same field. Which quality issue exists?
options: Ambiguity only
Redundancy only
Scope creep
Inconsistency that must be resolved before baselining
items.explanation: Contradictory statements about the same field are inconsistent and must be resolved before baselining. This is not mere ambiguity, redundancy, or scope creep, although consistency is at risk.

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of a requirements traceability matrix?
options: To link requirements to their sources, design, tests, and value throughout the lifecycle
To track the project budget
To list team members and their roles
To schedule deployment windows
items.explanation: A traceability matrix links requirements to sources, design, tests, and value across the lifecycle. Budget, staffing, and deployment scheduling are handled by other project artifacts.

items.stem: Once requirements are approved and agreed, what does baselining them provide?
options: A replacement for the business case
An agreed reference point against which changes are managed
A guarantee that no changes will ever occur
A substitute for testing
items.explanation: A baseline is the agreed reference for managing change. It does not guarantee no change, replace testing, or substitute for the business case, all of which serve different purposes.

items.stem: A stakeholder requests a change to a baselined requirement. What should the business analyst do FIRST?
options: Reject the change without review
Baseline a new version silently
Assess the impact of the change and route it through the change control process
Implement the change immediately
items.explanation: Changes are assessed for impact and routed through change control first. Immediate implementation, unreviewed rejection, and silent re-baselining bypass the process and hide consequences.

items.stem: Information such as owner, priority, status, and source is recorded for each requirement. What are these called?
options: Acceptance criteria
Business rules
Assumptions
Requirement attributes
items.explanation: Owner, priority, status, and source are requirement attributes used for management. Acceptance criteria define satisfaction, while business rules and assumptions are different concepts.

items.stem: A project assumes that the vendor's API will remain stable, and it must also use an older database version. Which term applies to each?
options: The stable API is an assumption and the database version is a constraint
Both are constraints
Both are assumptions
Both are benefits
items.explanation: A belief that must hold true is an assumption, while a fixed limitation is a constraint. Calling both the same ignores the difference between what is presumed and what is imposed.

items.stem: A requirement cannot be implemented unless another requirement is delivered first. What is this relationship called?
options: An out-of-scope requirement
A dependency between requirements
A conflict between requirements
A duplicate requirement
items.explanation: A sequential prerequisite relationship is a dependency. Conflict, duplication, and out-of-scope describe other relationships and are not the same as one requirement depending on another.

items.stem: Several solution options must be compared against weighted criteria such as cost, risk, and fit. Which technique is appropriate?
options: A burn-down chart
A control chart
A decision matrix or weighted scoring model
A fishbone diagram
items.explanation: A weighted decision matrix compares options against criteria transparently. Fishbone, burn-down, and control charts analyze causes, progress, and process stability rather than option selection.

items.stem: The business analyst compares the requirements to what the proposed solution will actually deliver. What is being analyzed?
options: The project's cost variance
The team's velocity
The number of defects
The gap between required capabilities and the proposed solution
items.explanation: Comparing requirements to what a solution delivers reveals the capability gap. Cost variance, velocity, and defect counts measure project performance rather than solution-requirement fit.

items.stem: Leadership wants to choose among build, buy, and reuse options for a capability. What should the business analyst perform?
options: A solution options analysis comparing each alternative's costs, benefits, and risks
A network design review
A staffing plan
A test strategy
items.explanation: Build, buy, and reuse alternatives are weighed in a solution options analysis. Network design, staffing, and test strategy each address a subset rather than the comparison itself.

items.stem: A complex set of requirements must be broken into smaller, manageable pieces. Which approach is used?
options: Random assignment of requirements
Decomposition of requirements into smaller deliverable components
Consolidation of all requirements into one item
Elimination of all but one requirement
items.explanation: Decomposition breaks complex requirements into manageable, deliverable pieces. Consolidation, elimination, and random assignment do not reduce complexity in a controlled way.

items.stem: An interview reveals that users need a report that currently does not exist. Which step converts this into an analyzable requirement?
options: Ignore the need until testing
Ask the user to write the code
Derive, document, and analyze candidate requirements from the elicited information
Send the interview notes straight to developers as final specification
items.explanation: Elicited information is converted into candidate requirements through derivation, documentation, and analysis. Raw notes, neglect, or asking users to code do not produce analyzed requirements.

items.stem: The business analyst documents the current process and the desired process side by side. What is this analysis called?
options: Cost-benefit analysis
Data migration
Risk analysis
As-is and to-be process modeling
items.explanation: Comparing the current and desired process is as-is and to-be modeling. Cost-benefit, data migration, and risk analysis are separate activities that do not compare process states.

items.stem: A requirement from a previous project is almost identical to a current need. What should the business analyst do?
options: Evaluate whether the existing requirement can be reused and adapted with stakeholder agreement
Copy it blindly without review
Reject it because it is old
Create a duplicate from scratch
items.explanation: Existing requirements may be reused after evaluation and stakeholder agreement. Blind copying, age-based rejection, and needless duplication ignore the potential for efficient reuse.

items.stem: Requirements must be organized for stakeholder review and approval. What should the business analyst produce?
options: A financial statement
A structured requirements package such as a requirements document or backlog
A resource-loaded schedule
A test log
items.explanation: Organizing requirements for review means producing a structured requirements package or backlog. Schedules, test logs, and financial statements do not present requirements for approval.

items.stem: Who should approve the analyzed and documented requirements?
options: The tester who will verify them
The infrastructure team
The authorized business stakeholders who own the need
The business analyst alone
items.explanation: Requirements are approved by the authorized business stakeholders who own the need. Analysts alone, testers, and infrastructure teams contribute but do not hold approval authority for business needs.

items.stem: Two stakeholders disagree on the priority of a requirement. What should the business analyst do?
options: Let the highest-paid stakeholder decide
Average the two priorities numerically
Defer the decision indefinitely
Facilitate a decision based on value, risk, and strategic alignment
items.explanation: Prioritization disputes are resolved by reference to value, risk, and strategy. Pay, numeric averaging, and indefinite deferral are arbitrary and do not reflect business merit.

items.stem: A requirement conflicts with a regulatory constraint. What should the business analyst do?
options: Highlight the conflict and treat compliance as a non-negotiable constraint
Ignore the regulation
Document the requirement as approved anyway
Remove all compliance requirements
items.explanation: Regulatory requirements are non-negotiable, so conflicts must be surfaced and resolved in favor of compliance. Ignoring the rule, approving the conflict, or deleting controls creates legal exposure.

items.stem: A high-priority requirement has high technical risk. How should this be handled in prioritization?
options: Escalate the decision to the vendor
Balance value against technical risk and plan mitigation or sequencing accordingly
Ignore risk and prioritize purely by value
Discard the requirement entirely
items.explanation: High-value requirements with high risk need a balance of value against risk plus mitigation planning. Ignoring risk, discarding the requirement, or outsourcing the decision harms value delivery.

items.stem: An agile team regularly revisits and refines the backlog. What is the purpose of backlog refinement?
options: To replace testing
To eliminate stakeholder input
To continuously analyze, clarify, and re-prioritize requirements as understanding grows
To freeze the backlog permanently
items.explanation: Refinement continuously analyzes, clarifies, and re-prioritizes items as understanding grows. Freezing the backlog, replacing testing, and removing stakeholder input defeat the purpose of ongoing refinement.

items.stem: A requirement is written in the form of a role, a goal, and a benefit. What is this format called?
options: A business rule
A constraint
A use case scenario
A user story capturing role, goal, and benefit
items.explanation: The role, goal, and benefit format is a user story. A business rule, constraint, or use case scenario has a different structure and purpose in requirements documentation.

items.stem: A user story should be independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, and testable. What is this set of criteria called?
options: The INVEST criteria for good user stories
The RACI model
The MoSCoW method
The SMART goals framework
items.explanation: The set of independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, and testable criteria is INVEST. RACI, MoSCoW, and SMART describe roles, prioritization, and goal setting respectively.

items.stem: A large body of related user stories is grouped under a broader capability. What are these larger groupings called?
options: Baselines and versions
Epics or themes that group related stories
Defects and incidents
Risks and issues
items.explanation: Related stories are grouped into epics or themes. Defects, risks, and baselines are different backlog and management items and do not describe a large capability grouping.

items.stem: Requirements for how two systems exchange messages must be analyzed in detail. Which activity applies?
options: Benefits realization
Resource leveling
Interface and integration requirements analysis
Stakeholder classification
items.explanation: System-to-system message exchange is analyzed as interface and integration requirements. Stakeholder classification, benefits realization, and resource leveling address other concerns.

items.stem: Legacy data must be transferred to a new system with acceptable quality. Which requirements domain applies?
options: User interface styling requirements
Facilities requirements
Marketing requirements
Data migration or data conversion requirements
items.explanation: Transferring legacy data is a data migration or conversion concern. Interface styling, facilities, and marketing requirements do not describe how data is moved and validated.

items.stem: The solution must protect personal data and control access. Which class of requirements applies?
options: Security and privacy requirements
Performance requirements
Usability requirements
Portability requirements
items.explanation: Data protection and access control are security and privacy requirements. Performance, usability, and portability describe speed, ease of use, and environment flexibility instead.

items.stem: New legislation mandates certain controls in the solution. How should this be handled in analysis?
options: Assume the vendor will handle it automatically
Translate the regulation into verifiable compliance requirements with traceability
Treat it as an optional nice-to-have
Ignore it until audit time
items.explanation: Regulation is translated into verifiable, traceable compliance requirements. Treating it as optional, deferring to audit, or assuming vendor coverage risks non-compliance and penalties.

items.stem: During analysis, the business analyst identifies requirements that may not be achievable. What should be done?
options: Delete them silently
Blame the stakeholders
Assess feasibility with the team and stakeholders and adjust, defer, or document the risk
Approve them anyway and hope for the best
items.explanation: Infeasible requirements are assessed with the team and stakeholders, then adjusted, deferred, or recorded as risk. Approving on hope, silent deletion, and blame hide rather than manage the issue.

items.stem: A requirement delivers high value but is expensive. How should the business analyst advise the sponsor?
options: Decide unilaterally to drop it
Hide the cost to gain approval
Implement it without any discussion
Present the value, cost, and trade-offs so the sponsor can make an informed decision
items.explanation: The analyst presents value, cost, and trade-offs so the sponsor decides with full information. Unilateral dropping, hiding costs, and proceeding without discussion remove informed decision making.

items.stem: The business analyst must show how each requirement contributes to business objectives. What should be documented?
options: The linkage from each requirement to the objectives and value it supports
The requirement's font style
The developer assigned to it
The test environment name
items.explanation: Documenting how requirements link to objectives and value demonstrates contribution. Styling, assignee, and environment names are irrelevant to showing business value alignment.

items.stem: A scoring model is used to prioritize requirements by value, cost, and risk. What does this produce?
options: A replacement for stakeholder input
A transparent, repeatable ranking to guide decisions
An exact prediction of project success
A guarantee that no changes will occur
items.explanation: A scoring model produces a transparent and repeatable ranking. It cannot promise success or freeze change and does not replace the judgment and input of stakeholders.

items.stem: Requirements are reviewed together by peers to find defects early. What is this practice?
options: A network scan
A budget audit
A formal requirements review or inspection
A post-implementation review
items.explanation: Peer examination of requirements to find defects early is a formal review or inspection. Post-implementation reviews, network scans, and budget audits occur for different reasons and times.

items.stem: Ambiguous requirements survived review. What is the MOST effective way to resolve them?
options: Let developers interpret them as they wish
Add more ambiguous detail
Remove all explanatory information
Meet with the source stakeholders to clarify intent and rewrite the requirement precisely
items.explanation: Ambiguity is resolved with the source stakeholders so intent is clarified and rewritten precisely. Developer guesswork, added vagueness, and removing context leave the ambiguity in place.

items.stem: Requirements change frequently during the project. How should these changes be managed?
options: Through version control and a defined change control process
By overwriting the original requirements without record
By ignoring the changes
By freezing all change permanently
items.explanation: Frequent change is managed with version control and a defined change control process. Overwriting without record, ignoring change, and permanent freezing all lose control or block necessary evolution.

items.stem: Developers and testers need to understand the requirements clearly. What should the business analyst ensure?
options: That requirements are written after development
That requirements are communicated in a form both groups can use to design and test
That requirements are kept secret until delivery
That only the business analyst reads them
items.explanation: Requirements must reach developers and testers in a usable form so they can design and verify. Secrecy, analyst-only access, and post-development documentation prevent that essential communication.

items.stem: A requirement is technically elegant but delivers no measurable business value. What should the business analyst do?
options: Add it to increase scope
Prioritize it above all others
Challenge the requirement and confirm whether it supports a real business need
Approve it because it is technically sound
items.explanation: Requirements must trace to real business value, so a technically elegant item with no value should be challenged. Approving it, adding scope, or over-prioritizing it wastes effort on low-value work.

items.stem: The business analyst must ensure requirements remain aligned with the business case as changes occur. What is the BEST practice?
options: Assume alignment never changes
Review alignment only at project closure
Delegate alignment checking to the vendor
Continuously trace and reassess requirements against objectives and value
items.explanation: Alignment is maintained by continuously tracing and reassessing requirements against objectives and value. Assumed alignment, closure-only review, and vendor delegation let drift go unnoticed.

items.stem: A set of requirements is complete and consistent, and stakeholders have agreed. What is the NEXT logical step?
options: Baseline the requirements and support solution design and delivery
Immediately declare the project complete
Stop documenting and disband the team
Delete the traceability matrix
items.explanation: Once agreed, requirements are baselined and used to support design and delivery. Declaring completion, disbanding, or deleting traceability skips design, build, and verification work.

items.stem: Before a solution is released, measures of success should already exist. What should the business analyst define?
options: The office seating plan
Performance measures and key indicators tied to the business objectives
The software license cost
The developers' names
items.explanation: Success measures and key indicators linked to objectives must be defined before release. Licensing, staffing names, and facilities do not measure whether the solution achieves its purpose.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A solution has been deployed. What is the purpose of solution evaluation?
options: To reassign the project team
To recreate the business case from scratch
To assess how well the solution meets business needs and delivers expected value
To rewrite the requirements
items.explanation: Solution evaluation assesses how well the deployed solution meets needs and delivers value. Rewriting requirements, reassigning staff, and rebuilding the business case are not the purpose of evaluation.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Executives want to know whether the solution achieved the benefits promised in the business case. What should the business analyst do?
options: Assume the benefits were achieved
Compare only the project budget
Ask the vendor for a certificate
Compare measured outcomes against the business case and report variances
items.explanation: Benefits are verified by comparing measured outcomes to the business case and reporting variances. Assumptions, budget-only comparison, and vendor certificates do not demonstrate realized benefits.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation
