items.stem: Benefits are realized only if they are actually measured and used. What does benefits realization management focus on?
options: Ensuring the intended benefits are achieved and tracked after delivery
Counting the number of features built
Reducing the project headcount
Extending the schedule
items.explanation: Benefits realization management ensures intended benefits are achieved and tracked after delivery. Feature counts, headcount, and schedule length do not confirm value is realized in operations.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A solution is tested against the conditions required for acceptance. What are these conditions derived from?
options: The project's meeting minutes
The agreed acceptance criteria and requirements
The vendor's marketing claims
The developer's preferences
items.explanation: Acceptance conditions are derived from agreed acceptance criteria and requirements. Marketing claims, developer preferences, and meeting minutes are not authoritative sources for acceptance.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Users report that a new system is slow and frustrating even though it meets the written requirements. What should the business analyst do FIRST?
options: Immediately rebuild the system
Close the project as successful
Investigate the root cause of the performance gap before recommending action
Blame the users for not adapting
items.explanation: Evaluation should first investigate the root cause of the performance gap. Blaming users, rebuilding without diagnosis, and declaring success ignore the evidence and risk the wrong response.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Evaluation shows that a solution is underperforming. What should the business analyst recommend?
options: Do nothing and wait
Abandon the solution without analysis
Ignore the data
Corrective actions based on evidence, with an assessment of options and impacts
items.explanation: Evidence-based corrective actions with assessed options and impacts are recommended. Inaction, abandonment without analysis, and ignoring data all prevent the organization from recovering value.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A solution reaches the end of its useful life and no longer provides value. What should the business analyst recommend?
options: Assess options to enhance, replace, or retire the solution based on value
Continue using it regardless of value
Increase its cost without analysis
Hide the decline from stakeholders
items.explanation: When value declines, the analyst assesses options to enhance, replace, or retire the solution. Continuing regardless, raising costs, or concealing decline wastes resources and misleads stakeholders.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: After a solution is delivered, what is the purpose of a lessons-learned activity?
options: To justify more budget
To capture what worked and what did not so future efforts improve
To assign blame for failures
To extend the project timeline
items.explanation: Lessons learned capture successes and problems to improve future work. Blame, timeline extension, and budget justification are not the intent and undermine honest reflection.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A post-implementation review is conducted months after go-live. What does it typically assess?
options: The vendor's stock price
The team's holiday schedule
Whether the solution delivered the expected benefits and how it is performing in operation
The accuracy of the original timesheets
items.explanation: A post-implementation review assesses benefit delivery and operational performance. Timesheets, vendor stock, and holiday schedules are unrelated to whether the solution achieved its intended outcomes.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: End users formally verify that the solution meets their needs before go-live. What is this activity?
options: Unit testing by developers
Code review
Load testing by operations
User acceptance testing and sign-off
items.explanation: End users formally verifying that their needs are met is user acceptance testing and sign-off. Unit tests, code reviews, and load tests are technical checks performed by the delivery team.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Leadership must decide whether to proceed to full deployment after a pilot. What decision is being made?
options: A go or no-go decision based on evaluation evidence
A budget reforecast only
A staffing decision
A marketing decision
items.explanation: Deciding to proceed after a pilot is a go or no-go decision grounded in evaluation evidence. Budget, staffing, and marketing decisions may follow but do not define the deployment gate.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A new solution must move from the project team to the operations group. What must be ensured?
options: That the project team keeps all knowledge
A structured transition including training, documentation, and support handover
An abrupt cutoff with no knowledge transfer
That operations is not informed
items.explanation: Transition requires structured training, documentation, and support handover. Abrupt cutoff, uninformed operations, and hoarded knowledge cause service failures once the project team leaves.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Evaluation shows low usage even though the solution works technically. What should the business analyst investigate?
options: The developer's commute
The color of the corporate logo
Adoption barriers such as training, usability, communication, or resistance
The server room temperature
items.explanation: Low usage despite technical function points to adoption barriers like training, usability, communication, or resistance. Environmental, personal, and cosmetic factors do not explain user adoption.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: After delivery, the business analyst meets stakeholders to confirm that needs were satisfied. What is being confirmed?
options: That the budget was fully spent
That no changes occurred
That the team is disbanded
That the solution validated against the original business needs and expectations
items.explanation: Confirming with stakeholders validates that the solution satisfies the original needs and expectations. Spending the budget, avoiding change, and disbanding the team are not measures of need satisfaction.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A solution improves one metric but harms another. What should the business analyst assess?
options: Unintended consequences and net impact across affected areas
Only the improved metric
Only the cost of the solution
The vendor's satisfaction
items.explanation: Evaluation must weigh unintended consequences and net impact across areas. Looking only at the improved metric, cost, or vendor satisfaction hides the harm and distorts the true effect.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: To evaluate a solution fairly, performance should be compared against what?
options: A single anecdote from one user
An agreed baseline and target measures established before or at delivery
The business analyst's intuition
The largest number reported anywhere
items.explanation: Fair evaluation compares performance to an agreed baseline and target measures. Intuition, the largest available number, and single anecdotes are not valid or comparable benchmarks.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: What should guide the collection of data for solution evaluation?
options: Only data that supports a favorable conclusion
A single informal conversation
Defined measures, reliable data sources, and a consistent collection method
Whatever data is easiest to find
items.explanation: Evaluation data should come from defined measures, reliable sources, and a consistent method. Convenience sampling, selective favorable data, and informal conversations produce biased conclusions.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Why does the timing of solution evaluation matter?
options: Evaluation should happen only once, immediately at go-live
Timing never affects results
Evaluation should always be postponed indefinitely
Benefits and performance may emerge over time, so evaluation should occur at appropriate intervals
items.explanation: Benefits often emerge over time, so evaluation is scheduled at appropriate intervals. One-time immediate review, ignoring timing, and indefinite postponement all miss the point of when value appears.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Several candidate solutions were evaluated and one was selected. What should be documented about the others?
options: The rationale for why they were not selected and the trade-offs considered
Nothing, because alternatives are irrelevant
Only their marketing materials
A guarantee they will never be reconsidered
items.explanation: Documenting why alternatives were not selected and the trade-offs preserves the decision rationale. Recording nothing, using marketing only, or foreclosing reconsideration reduces decision transparency.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: The business analyst compares value delivered to value planned. What is being measured?
options: The cost of training materials
The gap between expected and actual benefits of the solution
The number of meetings held
The team's velocity
items.explanation: Comparing delivered to planned value measures the benefits gap. Meeting counts, velocity, and training costs do not indicate whether the solution delivered the value that was expected.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Stakeholder satisfaction with a delivered solution needs to be gauged. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Counting only positive comments
Waiting for complaints
Structured surveys or interviews against defined satisfaction measures
Ignoring feedback and assuming satisfaction
items.explanation: Structured surveys or interviews against defined measures gauge satisfaction reliably. Assumption, counting only positives, and waiting for complaints produce a skewed or absent picture.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Operations data such as uptime, response time, and error rate is reviewed after deployment. What is being assessed?
options: The project's staffing plan
The marketing strategy
The organizational chart
The operational performance of the solution against its targets
items.explanation: Uptime, response time, and error rate assess operational performance against targets. Staffing plans, marketing strategy, and org charts are unrelated to runtime solution performance.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Evaluation identifies opportunities to improve a solution incrementally. What should the business analyst recommend?
options: A continuous improvement plan with prioritized, measurable enhancements
A complete rebuild every time
No further action ever
Removing the measurement system
items.explanation: Incremental improvement is captured in a continuous improvement plan with prioritized, measurable enhancements. Perpetual rebuilds, permanent inaction, and removing measurement waste or block improvement.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: What should happen to the results of a solution evaluation?
options: They should be used only to assign blame
They should be documented and communicated to stakeholders to support decisions
They should be discarded after the meeting
They should be kept secret from the sponsor
items.explanation: Evaluation results are documented and communicated so stakeholders can make informed decisions. Discarding, concealing, and using results for blame prevent the findings from creating value.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Stakeholders feel the new solution does not match what they expected. What should the business analyst do?
options: Ignore the feedback
Immediately terminate the project
Gather structured feedback, compare it to requirements and expectations, and recommend action
Tell stakeholders their expectations were wrong
items.explanation: The analyst gathers structured feedback and compares it to requirements and expectations before recommending action. Dismissing, ignoring, or terminating without analysis are premature or unhelpful responses.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A review reveals that expected benefits were never tracked. What should the business analyst recommend?
options: Assume the benefits were achieved anyway
Write off the project as a loss without evidence
Remove the benefits from the business case
Establish benefit measures and assign ownership so value can be confirmed
items.explanation: Untracked benefits require establishing measures and assigning ownership so value can be confirmed. Assuming success, unjustified write-off, and deleting benefits from the case hide the truth.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: The business analyst must present evaluation findings to the sponsor with a recommendation. What makes the recommendation credible?
options: Evidence from measured data and a clear link to business objectives
A confident tone without data
The support of the loudest stakeholder
A promise of future success
items.explanation: Credible recommendations rest on measured evidence linked to business objectives. Confident tone, loudest-voice support, and future promises are not substitutes for data-driven analysis.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: Who should own the continued realization of benefits after the project closes?
options: The project's tester
The business owner or benefits owner accountable for the outcome
The business analyst permanently
The software vendor
items.explanation: The business or benefits owner remains accountable for realizing value after closure. Analysts, vendors, and testers have defined roles but do not own the ongoing benefits outcome.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation

items.stem: A solution meets its functional requirements but no longer supports the organization's strategy. What should the business analyst conclude?
options: Strategy should be changed to match the solution
No action is ever needed
The solution may need to be enhanced, replaced, or retired to stay aligned with strategy
The solution is perfect because requirements were met
items.explanation: A solution must continue to support strategy, so declining alignment calls for enhancement, replacement, or retirement. Meeting requirements, changing strategy to fit, and taking no action ignore strategic value.
items.reference: PMI-PBA Exam Content Outline - Solution Evaluation
